items.title: Ioannidis argued most published research findings are false
items.claim: John Ioannidis's 2005 PLoS Medicine paper made what claim?

options.text: Most published research findings are false — because of low prior probability of true effects, low power, flexibility in analysis, and selective reporting; the title was 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'

items.reveal:
Ioannidis used a Bayesian framework: a positive finding's probability of being true depends on prior probability of the hypothesis, power, type I error rate and bias. For exploratory research with many tested hypotheses and small studies, the probability that a 'significant' result is true can be below 50%.

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper directly tested this in psychology: of 100 replications, 36% were significant in the same direction as the original. Effect sizes averaged about half the original. Hardly any of those original findings were obviously wrong; many were inflated by methodological flexibility.
items.why: The replication crisis isn't unique to psychology — it has hit medicine, economics, marketing and machine learning. The methodological response (preregistration, larger samples, registered reports) is reshaping research practice.

items.title: Milgram's obedience rate
items.claim: In Stanley Milgram's 1963 baseline experiment, participants were ordered to deliver what they believed were increasing electric shocks to a stranger. What proportion went all the way to the maximum 450 volts?
items.reveal_title: Around 65% continued to the maximum level
items.reveal:
In Milgram's original Yale study (1963), 26 of 40 participants (65%) continued to the 450V switch under verbal pressure from the experimenter.

Replications, including Burger (2009) in modified form, found broadly similar obedience patterns.
items.why: Situational pressure from a perceived authority figure can override personal moral judgement to a degree most people predict incorrectly.

items.title: Effect size matters as much as significance
items.claim: A study reports a 'highly significant' effect (p < 0.001) of a school intervention. What further information do you need?

options.text: The effect size (e.g. Cohen's d, standardised mean difference). A trivial effect can be highly significant with a large sample; a substantial effect can be non-significant with a small sample. Significance and magnitude are different questions
Only the title of the paper

items.reveal:
Cohen's d conventions (1988): 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Education research (EEF, Hattie's meta-analyses) often reports effect sizes in months of additional learning progress.

The ASA Statement on p-values (2016) explicitly warned against treating p < 0.05 as sufficient. Recommendations: report effect sizes with confidence intervals; treat 'significance' as one piece of evidence, not as a binary verdict.
items.why: Newspaper science writing usually reports significance, not magnitude. The interesting question for policy or practice is almost always how big the effect is.
